interviewQuestions.question: Why do Vision Transformers need more data than CNNs to shine?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd frame this around inductive bias. A CNN's convolutional filters bake in two assumptions before training even starts: nearby pixels tend to be related (locality), and a useful feature detector should work the same way regardless of where in the image it appears (translation invariance). Those assumptions happen to be true of natural images, so the CNN gets a meaningful head start and can learn effectively even from a modest dataset. A ViT makes no such built-in assumption — every patch attends globally to every other patch from the first layer, so the model has to discover on its own, purely from data, that nearby patches are usually related. That's a strictly harder learning problem, and with too little data the ViT often doesn't discover it well, landing below a comparable CNN. Give it enough data, though (hundreds of millions of images, as in the original ViT paper), and it not only catches up but surpasses CNNs, because it isn't limited by an assumption that's only approximately true — it can learn a more accurate model of spatial structure directly from data. Concretely: this is why, in practice, you rarely train a ViT from scratch on a modest dataset — you either use a CNN, or you fine-tune a large-scale pretrained ViT checkpoint, letting the pretraining supply the spatial understanding a small dataset can't.

**Testing:** whether you understand inductive bias as a concrete trade-off (a head start that caps eventual performance) rather than a vague "ViTs are newer so they need more data" claim.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Inductive bias as a data-efficiency trade-off

interviewQuestions.question: How does a Vision Transformer turn an image into something a Transformer can actually process?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
A standard Transformer expects a sequence of token embeddings, and an image is a 2D grid of pixels — ViT bridges that gap with a fairly mechanical patchify step. The image is split into fixed-size, non-overlapping patches (16×16 pixels is the classic choice), each patch is flattened into a single long vector, and that vector is linearly projected into an embedding of the model's working dimension — exactly the same role a word embedding plays for a token in NLP. A learned positional encoding is added to each patch embedding so the model knows where in the image each patch came from, since the sequence itself has no spatial layout once flattened.

The resulting sequence of patch embeddings feeds through standard Transformer encoder blocks — self-attention lets every patch attend to every other patch directly, regardless of distance, which is the key structural difference from a CNN: a convolution only sees a small local neighborhood per layer and builds up long-range relationships gradually across many layers, while a ViT's first layer already has global receptive field.

A 224×224 image with 16×16 patches produces 196 patch tokens (plus often a special classification token), which is a manageable sequence length — this patch size is itself a real trade-off: smaller patches mean finer spatial resolution but a much longer, more expensive sequence, since attention cost grows quadratically with sequence length.

**Testing:** whether you can walk through the actual patchify-and-embed mechanism, not just say "it splits the image into patches."
interviewQuestions.subTitle: How ViT tokenizes an image

interviewQuestions.question: What's actually happening in a CLIP-style model that lets it classify images into categories it's never seen labeled examples of?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Zero-shot classification works because CLIP was never trained to predict fixed class labels in the first place — it was trained to learn one shared embedding space for images and text, using millions of naturally-occurring (image, caption) pairs scraped from the web, with a contrastive objective that pulls a matching image-caption pair's embeddings close together and pushes mismatched pairs apart. Nothing about that training references a fixed taxonomy of classes; it just learns that a photo of a golden retriever and the text "a photo of a golden retriever" should land near each other in embedding space, for every pair it saw.

At inference time, "classification" becomes a search problem, not a lookup in a trained classifier head: embed the image once, embed each candidate class name as a short text template ("a photo of a {class}"), and pick whichever text embedding is closest to the image embedding by cosine similarity. Since any new class is just a new string to embed, the model can be handed a completely novel set of categories at inference time it never explicitly trained on — that's the entire mechanism behind "zero-shot."

The practical limit: performance depends heavily on how well the class name's *phrasing* matches the kind of captions in training data — an unusual or highly technical class name can embed poorly even if the model has implicitly "seen" the visual concept, which is why prompt templates for the class names matter more than people expect.

**Testing:** whether you understand zero-shot classification as embedding-space nearest-neighbor search enabled by contrastive pretraining, not a special classification mode.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: How zero-shot classification actually works
